claims.text: The target material is the dual-nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy.
The initial alloy is additive-manufactured and contains well-dispersed nanoscale precipitates in a high-entropy matrix.
In situ TEM combined with spatially resolved EDX/EELS can be used to study the target alloy during controlled high-temperature oxidation.
The proposed oxidation temperature range is 800–1100 °C under controlled oxygen partial pressure.
The dual nanoprecipitates are the structural mediator of oxidation behavior.
High-temperature oxidation will produce dynamic, localized elemental redistribution at the nanoprecipitates.
Oxidation promotes elemental migration from nanoprecipitates into the surrounding matrix and evolving oxide scale.
Elemental redistribution modifies the local chemistry around nanoprecipitates.
Local elemental redistribution changes the kinetics of oxide formation.
Elemental redistribution can change whether the resulting oxide scale is protective.
Al-rich or Cr-rich oxide layers are examples of potentially protective scales in the target alloy.
Spatially resolved EDX/EELS will reveal depletion or enrichment of Al, Ti, Cr, or other elements at and near nanoprecipitates.
Elemental shifts near nanoprecipitates will correlate with changes in oxide-scale morphology and chemistry.
Nanoprecipitate-associated redistribution will produce an observable increase or decrease in oxidation resistance relative to the baseline.
Prior cast or wrought and ex situ oxidation studies do not resolve nanoscale dynamic elemental redistribution during oxidation.
In situ observations in a TEM may not extrapolate directly to long-term oxidation outside the controlled microscope environment.
Electron-beam effects could influence oxidation behavior during TEM imaging.
Comparing nanoprecipitate-containing regions with nanoprecipitate-free regions can test whether nanoprecipitates mediate local oxide formation and elemental kinetics.
